extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policy makers, and practitioners interested in Indian pharmaceutical patent law and patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how Indian Patent Office examiners apply Section 3(d) and other patentability/prosecution criteria to pharmaceutical patent applications, using first examination reports (FERs) and prosecution histories. Focuses on claim-level application of 3(d), overlap with novelty/inventive step, outcomes, and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(d) — new forms require enhanced efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Text of Section 3(d): 'The mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in the enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance ... For the purposes of this clause, esters, ethers, polymorphs, metabolites, pure form, particle size, isomers, mixtures of isomers, complexes, combinations, and other derivatives of known substance shall be considered to be the same substance, unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented to limit 'secondary' patents and prevent evergreening; to obtain a patent on a new form of a known substance the applicant must demonstrate increased efficacy (often via comparative data). Applicants may rebut by arguing the claimed compound is genuinely new (not a derivative) or by providing comparative efficacy data. 3(d) intended as a higher bar for modifications (salts, esters, polymorphs, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (lack of novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional patentability requirement: claims must be novel over prior art; FERs commonly cite lack of novelty as a ground for objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often invoked together with 3(d); when novelty objections target claim 1 they frequently co-occur with 3(d) objections. Novelty may be applied to different claims than 3(d) within the same application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step / non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional patentability requirement that the claimed invention involves an inventive step (is not obvious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently used by IPO examiners alongside 3(d). Overlap at claim level is common: when 3(d) is raised on claim 1, novelty or inventive step is also raised against that claim in the vast majority of cases. Final refusal may be on lack of inventive step even if 3(d) was raised earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim 1 importance / claim-level targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim 1 is an independent claim and typically the broadest and most important claim; objections on claim 1 hit the core of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERs that explicitly target claim 1 with 3(d) (or novelty/inventive step) indicate examiners are striking the application's core. Analysis should distinguish objections 'on claim 1' vs. objections without specified claims because FER vagueness can obscure claim-level targeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: FER specificity vs ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: First Examination Reports (FERs) vary in specificity: some directly indicate which claims are objected to, others simply state 'claims fail to satisfy' without specifying claim numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous FER language is an anti-pattern for claim-level analysis; trend toward more specific FERs over time improves ability to attribute objections to particular claims. Analysts should code FERs as 'objection including claim 1', 'objection not directed at claim 1', or 'objection without specific claims'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural timing and response requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must request examination within 4 years after international priority date; FERs are typically issued within six months of examination; failure to respond to FER leads to abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural deadlines determine whether an application is classified as withdrawn, abandoned, refused or granted. Timing from FER to grant (grant lag) is an outcome metric; 3(d) presence in FERs is associated with longer grant lags and higher likelihood of abandonment or refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome categories for applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutually exclusive categories recorded: granted, pending (still awaiting final determination), withdrawn before examination, abandoned after a first examination report issued, or refused (applicant pursued but ultimately unsuccessful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories enable measurement of grant rates, abandonment behavior, and associations between objection types (3(d), novelty, inventive step) and final outcomes. For refused applications, full prosecution records (post-FER exchanges, hearings, Controller’s Decisions) are informative about grounds for final refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary vs secondary application classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary applications: include at least one claim on a new compound. Secondary applications: claims on polymorphs, crystal forms, enantiomers/isomers, salts, metabolites, derivatives, compositions, or uses of an existing compound (and not claiming new compound). Process-only applications are separate and often dropped from analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 3(d) was intended to target secondary patents (evergreening). Empirical coding of applications into primary/secondary is necessary to evaluate whether 3(d) is being applied as intended. Paper finds 3(d) is increasingly used on primary applications as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap/redundancy assessment between 3(d) and traditional grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether 3(d) objections co-occur with novelty or inventive step objections at the application and claim level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High co-occurrence (e.g., 67% of FERs cite both 3(d) and novelty/inventive step; 96% of FERs with 3(d) also have novelty/inventive step objections) suggests potential redundancy, but claim-level analysis is required to assess whether provisions target the same claims. Researchers should classify combinations and compare grant rates and lags by objection type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant rate and grant lag as evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical metrics: grant rate (share of applications ultimately granted) and time from FER to certificate of issue (grant lag).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess association between objection types and prosecution difficulty: applications with both 3(d) and novelty/inventive step objections have lower grant rates and longer grant lags. Compare grant rates across objection categories (e.g., neither objection, novelty/inventive step alone, 3(d) + novelty/inventive step) and test statistical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence burden under 3(d): comparative efficacy data and claim amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome 3(d), applicants may present comparative data demonstrating enhanced efficacy or amend/remove claims to render 3(d) inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many successful replies applicants argued the compound is genuinely new (thus 3(d) not relevant) or submitted comparative efficacy data. Preparing effective replies requires time and resources; inability or unwillingness to pursue this can lead to abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 3(d) on primary patents (expanded application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical observation that 3(d) is increasingly invoked against primary patent applications (new compound claims) contrary to its original intent to target secondary patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expanded application has policy implications: if 3(d) is read to cover primary patents, India’s system could reduce patenting of truly new drugs. Analysts should track shares of primary vs secondary applications with 3(d) objections on claim 1 over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner behavior, guidelines, and legal environment as implicit criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners' propensity to use 3(d) depends on examination guidelines, training, and legal precedents (e.g., Supreme Court or Appellate Board decisions), as well as institutional pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in guidelines or judicial rulings can increase examiners' confidence in invoking 3(d). Variation across examiners can confound causal interpretation of 3(d)'s independent effect; researchers should consider examiner-level heterogeneity and policy shifts when assessing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: FER-driven downstream scrutiny (indirect effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking 3(d) early in examination may trigger deeper subsequent scrutiny, revealing other deficiencies (novelty/inventive step) and influencing applicant decisions to abandon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 3(d) may have indirect effects similar to deferred examination rules by prompting applicants to drop weak applications; distinguishing direct from indirect effects requires careful analysis of prosecution histories and possibly exogenous variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity/limitations of available data (coding and measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: FER quality varies over time; earlier FERs often vague, later FERs more specific. Data truncation (e.g., Indian data truncated to 2012 at the time of collection) and missing final decisions for many FERs limit inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should document coding rules, sample restrictions (e.g., PCT July priority month), and account for censoring when interpreting trends in FER prevalence, claim-level attribution, and grant rates.
